feedback: When a card is binned, state the reason: 'both quantities increase together in a constant ratio → direct' or 'one increases while the other decreases with a constant product (doubling one halves the other) → inverse.'
If a rate is tagged without units or with wrong units, prompt the X-per-Y form (miles per hour, kg per cubic metre).

Reinforce that 'neither' is a real category — not every 'more → more' situation is direct and not every 'more → less' situation is inverse; two quantities can both rise without a constant ratio, or one can fall as the other rises without a constant product.
activities.intendedInsight: The boundary between direct, inverse, and non-proportional situations becomes visible through contrasting examples and non-examples; every rate carries units.
learnerActions: Sort situation cards into three bins: direct proportion, inverse proportion, and neither (non-proportional).
Attach the correct unit tag to each rate card (speed = mph or m/s; density = kg/m³).
Complete sentence frames using the vocabulary, e.g. 'as … increases, … so this is … proportion.'
Read the feedback that names the tell ('both increase together in a constant ratio → direct') and re-sort any you placed wrongly.
activities.title: Sort-and-tag: direct / inverse / neither, with unit tags

feedback: Check that each map includes a genuine non-example, not just an example reworded.
If 'scale factor' is described as 'add 3', correct it to a multiplier ('×3').

Tie the mathematical meaning of 'direct proportion' to 'as one changes, the other changes in a constant ratio', and of 'inverse proportion' to 'as one changes, the other changes so that their product stays constant.'
activities.intendedInsight: Each term has a fenced meaning with clear examples, non-examples, and (for rates) units; 'proportion' and 'scale factor' have specific mathematical senses distinct from loose everyday use.
learnerActions: For each term (direct proportion, inverse proportion, ratio, rate, unit rate, compound unit, scale factor), fill a four-box map: definition, characteristics, an example, and a non-example.
Add the units for each rate/compound measure (speed: mph or m/s; density: kg/m³).
Explicitly contrast the everyday sense of 'proportion' (an amount) with the mathematical sense (a multiplicative part-to-whole relationship / constant ratio).
Note that 'scale factor' is a MULTIPLIER, not an additive change.
activities.title: Frayer-style term map (reference and consolidation)

feedback: If both situations are called 'direct', have the learner say which way EACH quantity moves and whether doubling one halves the other; opposite movement with a constant product → inverse. Re-sort more example/non-example pairs rehearsing 'as … doubles, … halves, so inverse', including opposite-moving non-examples that are neither.
If 60 mph is called 'a ratio' or a 'rate' without units, insist on the X-per-Y units and explain a rate is a ratio of two different quantities with units.
If the learner can label but not generate a fresh inverse example, their use is recognitional, not yet productive — prompt for a new everyday situation.
activities.intendedInsight: Real command shows in how you USE the words in an explaining sentence and in whether you can PRODUCE a correct fresh example — not in label-matching.
learnerActions: Given two situations — (1) the more workers dig the trench, the less time it takes (assume every worker digs at the same rate); (2) the more petrol you buy, the more it costs (at a fixed price per litre) — state for EACH whether the quantities are in direct or inverse proportion and say a sentence explaining why.
For a car travelling 120 miles in 2 hours, state what '60 miles per hour' is called and what makes it that (a rate/speed, a compound unit comparing distance to time, miles PER hour).
Generate your OWN fresh example of an inverse proportion and your own example of a direct proportion.
Distinguish 'rate' from 'ratio': a rate is a ratio of two DIFFERENT quantities carrying units (X per Y).
activities.title: Check and probe: use the words, generate your own examples
